item.title: Musk takes 'crusade' to Europe with Armie Hammer film
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4w5nwk00o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Musk takes 'crusade' to Europe with Armie Hammer film - Published An American vigilante tears across an unnamed European country, killing dozens of police officers and judges, slaughtering a gang of rapists, and killing a refugee family and a random civilian – all in the name of a crusade against Muslim migrants and "woke" government officials. Citizen Vigilante, a film from German director Uwe Boll and starring actor Armie Hammer, is violent – and very schlocky – stuff. Initially denied a rating by German's film regulator, it would likely have garnered very little attention, had it not caught the eye of the world's richest person. Elon Musk made the film free to view via his social media platform X for 48 hours in late June, and the subsequent attention briefly pushed the movie into the top of the charts of several streaming providers including Apple and Amazon. At one point he reposted a message about the film that described vigilante murder as the "moderate response" to violent crimes committed by immigrants. It's just one of many recent examples of the tech titan's increasing interest in extreme ideas and activists, and in particular his support of political parties and politicians on the right in Europe. Musk left the Trump administration more than a year ago and his Doge project, which aimed to slash the size of the US federal government, has since been wound down. But he has recently sought to conquer other political territory. "This is a crusade," says Georgios Samaras, an assistant professor of public policy at King's College London who studies the European and US far right. "Musk uses the power he has to amplify the ideas that he thinks should dominate society. He knows he has the money and he knows he has the influence." 'Radicalised by his own network' Much of that influence comes via X, formerly Twitter, the social media platform that Musk bought outright in 2022. Since stripping away many of the old Twitter's content moderation rules - derided as censorship by Musk and others - the network has become a haven for far-right beliefs and conspiracy theories. In turn, X appears to have shaped Musk. Although it's difficult to glean a cohesive worldview from social media fragments - Musk did not respond to requests for comment for this story - his output has demonstrated a growing obsession with race and white people in particular. He has posted and reposted a slew of messages - often from white nationalist and far-right activists - portraying white people as under threat, including messages like "Whites are a rapidly dying minority" and "If White men become a minority, we will be slaughtered". He has endorsed the leader of France's hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen. "She is France's last hope," he wrote. Musk also recently reposted a video from the far-right activist Tommy Robinson that suggested police are going easy on criminals if they have brown skin, with the comment "literally true". He's also boosted right-wing politicians and parties in Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and the UK. Although at one point he toyed with donating huge sums of money to Reform UK, he since broke with Nigel Farage over Farage's shunning of Robinson, and more recently has boosted the profile of Rupert Lowe's breakaway party Restore Britain – a Reform rival that seeks to take an even tougher line on immigration. In June, after a Sudanese man was accused of a brutal stabbing in Northern Ireland, Musk shared a list of street protest locations posted by Robinson, adding: "Only by protesting REPEATEDY and LOUDLY will there be any change!!" In other posts he claimed that former Prime Minister Keir Starmer "hates white people" and shared an image of the stabbing suspect with the comment "millions must go". Mobs rioted on the streets of Belfast, where the stabbing happened. Police highlighted the role of social media in co-ordinating the disorder. The Center for Countering Digital Hate, a research and advocacy group that has been the target of legal action by Musk in the past, tallied 4,000 calls for violence on X written as responses underneath posts by Musk, Lowe and Robinson. "Many people on the right use Musk as a means to an end," says AJA Woods, a historian studying conspiracy theories and reactionary politics. "He's seen as a source of funds, or someone who's in control of X so can be used to promote their ideas… he's a convenient ally." When contacted for comment, Lowe described the CCDH report as "embarrassing guff" and called the BBC a "disgrace". Remigration exported Despite being in charge of several enormous companies, Musk regularly wades into ostensibly local disputes, not just in Belfast but across Europe, apparently gleaning much of his knowledge from people he follows on X. "You find a tutoring relationship, one in which Musk is inducted into their talking points," says Ben Tarnoff, co-author of Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed. One of those talking points is his embrace of the term "remigration". Anti-immigration advocates use it to refer to mass deportations, even of legal migrants. In its extreme form, it means the removal through force or heavy persuasion of all non-whites or foreigners, even if they were born in or and have deep roots in their home countries. Slightly more moderate versions focus on recent migrants or those not fully integrated into European societies. The concept has been linked to violent activity, experts say, and Musk and X have not only been instrumental in spreading the idea across Europe, but in importing it to the United States, Tarnoff says. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees US immigration, posted an X message consisting of one word: "Remigrate". "Something that Musk shares with members of the American right and particularly with Donald Trump's circle is a view of Europe and the UK as the ancestral home of white civilisation, but a home that has surrendered itself to the woke forces of multiculturalism," says Tarnoff. - What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack - Published17 hours ago
Saturday's attack at a Berlin Pride event - which was described by officials as an "Islamist terror attack" - gave far-right influencers that Musk converses with on X another opportunity to warn of civilizational collapse and call for drastic measures in response. Musk later wrote in response to a Spanish anti-immigration influencer: "Anyone who opposes remigration is a traitor". 'Astonishingly bad' and 'fascist propaganda' Citizen Vigilante was cheered by many far-right activists on X, even as others slammed the movie, not only for its politics but for its thin plot, cheap-looking special effects and abundance of gore. After the publicity boost, Boll estimated that the film made about $600,000 from streaming, against a budget of $2m. Critics were scathing. Variety called it "astonishingly bad" while prominent American conservative commentator Rod Dreher called it "fascist propaganda", although he and some others on the right defended its depiction of a Europe in turmoil. The film's portrayal of European society dovetails with the bleak vision pushed by Musk and others on the right – that citizens have been utterly betrayed by a corrupt establishment, that migrants are at the root of violence and chaos, and that extreme measures are needed to restore order. "People who are complaining that he spends the first half of the movie murdering white people not migrants fail to understand… Always hang a traitor before you shoot an enemy," read one message reposted by Musk. - 'Let's enjoy the ride' of AI, Musk tells The Economist - Published4 days ago
Challenged last week in an Economist interview on whether he was being irresponsible to promote a film which glorifies the murder of a Muslim family, Musk said: "It's a movie and it's worth watching." "I don't think Europe's a hell hole," he said, but also insisted that "there was out of control rape and murder." He also stood by previous statements that he believed civil war in the UK was "inevitable", and referring to Muslims, he said: "If you have a large and rapidly growing group of people whose beliefs are antithetical to Western beliefs, at some point there will be a reckoning." The tech titan also said he had not visited the UK in several years. Musk's defenders have often praised his professed support for unfettered online speech and have chalked some of his more extreme stances up to online exaggeration. Others say his influence over politics in the UK and Europe is limited. "I don't think he has much political sway in Britain or on the continent," says Gawain Towler, a former Reform UK director of communications who still supports the party. Towler says he credits Musk with highlighting rape gangs in British cities and says he is relaxed about the tycoon's support for Lowe and Restore. "I generally prefer the stuff he says about his businesses," he says. Related topics - Published3 September 2025

item.title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dng1v72lno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next? - Published In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct. So education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on Saturday, after more than a week of intense street protests, became a defining moment - one many young people celebrated as a rare victory. In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests". Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit. Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years". On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times. Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram." The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal. The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families. Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk. Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them. The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country. Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed. Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning". "For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says. Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage. Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded. "Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says. Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture. India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data. Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs. The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year. On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended. "I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices." Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over." A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next". But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension. Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees". But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations. Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40. Human Rights Watch says, external that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws". Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual". At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

item.title: The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0m8z6de3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold - Published The reigning 57kg world champion boxer Jaismine Lamboria from India throws punches for a living, but when it comes to handling pressure, she looks to one of her country's most celebrated cricketing legends for inspiration. "I really admire MS Dhoni's mindset," says the soft-spoken Lamboria of the former Indian captain. "He is known as 'Captain Cool' for a reason, and I want to be calm like him." That composure will be particularly valuable for Lamboria over the coming days. The 24-year-old is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, looking to improve on the bronze she won at Birmingham 2022. Coming off a breakout 2025 during which she won World Cup golds in Astana and Delhi before becoming world champion in Liverpool, Lamboria is in Glasgow with an uncomplicated ambition. "I aim to change the colour of that medal to gold," she says. "That's what I've been training and preparing towards." At 5ft 8½in, Lamboria is tall by Indian boxing standards. Her Olympic debut in Paris ended in a first-round defeat to Tokyo silver medallist Nesthy Petecio of the Philippines. But the setback came in the weight class she had only recently returned to. After spending nearly three years boxing at 60kg, Lamboria dropped back to 57kg during the Paris qualification campaign - a move that ultimately paid off when she won the world title by defeating Paris Olympic silver medallist Julia Atena Szeremeta of Poland. "That Paris 2024 Olympics exit was disappointing but it was an eye-opener," says Lamboria. "It prompted several changes in me - physically and mentally. And a significant part of it has come about at the Army Sports Institute (ASI) in Pune, which is where I train." Lamboria credits her ASI coaches for improving his physical strength and a motivational coach and sports psychologist for sharpening her mental game. The Indian Army, however, has provided the wider institutional framework around much of her development. After winning bronze at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Lamboria became the first female boxer inducted into the army, joining the Corps of Military Police. She now trains under its Mission Olympics Wing. "It's a great honour they wanted to begin with me, but I also see it as an opportunity to become a role model for female athletes," says Lamboria of joining a system that has produced Olympians and Paralympians, including Olympic javelin champion Neeraj Chopra. In early 2024, the Indian Army launched the Girls Sports Company to train girls aged 12 to 16 in four Olympic sports, including boxing, creating a pathway to elite competition and army recruitment. "These girl athletes are doing very well too," says Lamboria. "One boxer has already won Asian Championships gold, which makes me really happy. I may have been the first female boxer in the Indian Army, but I won't be the last." Lamboria's relationship with boxing, however, began long before the army entered her story. Born in the northern state of Haryana, she grew up in Bhiwani, a city synonymous with Indian boxing and widely nicknamed the country's 'Mini Cuba'. Her great-grandfather Hawa Singh was one of Indian boxing's early giants. A heavyweight, he won successive Asian Games gold medals in 1966 and 1970 and was among those who established the famed Bhiwani Boxing Club, which would later produce boxers including Olympic medallist Vijender Singh. Even so, it is not Hawa's medals that feature most prominently in the stories Lamboria remembers hearing about him at home. "He was powerful, but there was also so much humility in him," she says. Her earliest boxing influences were her uncles, Sandeep Singh and Parvinder Singh. "I grew up watching them compete," she says. "They were the ones who got me started." Lamboria began boxing seriously around the age of 14, training first at an academy run by Hawa's son, Sanjay Sheoran, before continuing under her uncles. Though the sport ran through her extended family, Lamboria grew up in a household of modest means. Her father, Jaiveer, works as a home guard, while her mother, Joginder, is a homemaker. "Their support has been a big reason why I was the first girl in my immediate family to take up sport seriously," she says, "not least as the youngest among the girls in the family." Her inspirations, meanwhile, extend well beyond her own family. Lamboria grew up idolising Olympic medallists MC Mary Kom and Vijender Singh. Later, she looked up to Indian Army boxers Amit Panghal and Manish Kaushik, Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, American swimming great Michael Phelps and Indian sprinting legend Milkha Singh. Closer to home, she credits senior Indian boxers Nikhat Zareen, Lovlina Borgohain and Pooja Rani, not just for their medals but for the encouragement they offer younger athletes. "When you look at them, you naturally feel that you want to do what they have done," she says. Now, Lamboria is beginning to occupy that role herself. "For a long time, boxing has been seen as a male-dominated sport," she says. "Being a woman boxer and an Army athlete, it means a lot to compete on the world stage, prove myself and inspire others through my performances." That change is reflected in the Commonwealth Games too. Boxing has been part of the event since 1930, but women's competition was introduced only in 2014. In Glasgow, bouts began on 24 July, with the finals on 31 July and 1 August. After winning bronze in Birmingham four years ago, Lamboria hopes to leave Glasgow with gold. "When you're competing overseas and the national anthem plays, it's a completely different feeling," she says. "I experienced that at the World Championships in Liverpool last year. That's the moment I want to recreate here."

item.title: Biden, Carney and Oasis: How the world is celebrating Mayo's All-Ireland win
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx74qw9ggjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Biden, Carney and Oasis: How the world is celebrating Mayo's All-Ireland win - Published What do a former US president, the Canadian prime minister and two of the world's biggest rock stars have in common? They're all celebrating after their Irish county Mayo overcame a 75-year-old 'curse' and finally broke its barren run in one of Ireland's biggest sporting occasions. Victory in the Gaelic Athletic Association's (GAA) All-Ireland Senior Football final had eluded Mayo for over seven decades until Sunday, when they overcame reigning champions Kerry. The celebrations have gone far beyond the county in the west of Ireland, which is home to just 137,000 people but boasts some very famous exports. Mayo for Sam The chant "Mayo for Sam" is well known in GAA circles, but three years ago it garnered its most famous endorsement yet - the president of the United States. It was shouted by Joe Biden as he visited his ancestral home in Ballina. The Sam to which he was referring is the Sam Maguire Cup - the prize for winning the All-Ireland Football final. Biden, who left office in January 2025 when Donald Trump became president, has never been shy about his Irish roots. - What does it mean to end 75 years of heartbreak? - Published15 hours ago
- Cursed? The story of the 72-year-old hex that haunts Mayo - Published6 December 2023
With two great-grandparents coming from Ireland, he is one of the most Irish presidents in history. And on Sunday, Biden took to social media to celebrate Mayo's victory. He congratulated the team on their win, proclaimed that the people of Mayo had earned the victory and reminded them to "enjoy every minute". And, of course, he repeated the all-important words: "Mayo for Sam!" When was the last time Mayo won the All-Ireland final? For some, Mayo's failure to win an All-Ireland football title for decades was proof of a curse dating all the way back to the early 1950s. It was in Ballina where, almost 100 years after Biden's ancestors had fled the devastating Irish potato famine, a supposed curse was placed on the Mayo Gaelic football team. The story - or myth - goes, that following their last win in 1951 the Mayo team's boisterous celebrations on an open-back lorry interrupted a funeral in the village of Foxford. The presiding priest is said to have laid a curse that Mayo would not win an All-Ireland title while any member of that team was alive. And despite reaching the final eleven times in the years to follow, they failed to win it. In April 2023, the last member of the Mayo 1951 panel, Dr Mick Loftus, passed away. Sean McAndrew, whose father John played for both the 1951 and 1951 winning Mayo teams, said it was "amazing" to watch the county reclaim the All-Ireland title. Sean said that although his dad moved moved to Birmingham in England in 1960, he always kept up to date with the team. "Mayo probably has one of the highest emigrant populations across the world and a lot of people see the GAA as their connection to home." John McAndrew passed away in 2013 and Sean said it would have meant a lot to him to see Mayo win again. "It's all he ever wanted and you could see the disappointment each time that they failed." Sean said there was "no talk" of a curse for the first few years after Mayo last won in 1951, "but then I think people got suspicious when good teams weren't progressing". He added that his dad was a "quiet, level-headed" man who didn't talk much about the curse, but had said he "couldn't recall" the supposed incident involving a funeral. Sean said he has always taken talk about a curse in "good humour", but does recall one occasion when a women approached him and his son after an unsuccessful final for Mayo and said "maybe we need to get rid of a few of them", referring to the surviving members of the 1951 team. "It did make you think twice about whether people believe in things… and thought that's what needed to be done," he said. Has the Mayo curse been lifted? On a Sunday afternoon in July 2026, Biden's words finally came true. The long wait for the county's fourth All-Ireland title was over and the Sam Maguire trophy would be heading for Mayo. It was an intense final that went down to the wire at a raucous Croke Park in Dublin. Mayo suffered a slow start, but they bounced back and a late score from Tommy Conroy sealed a famous win in front of a sold-out 82,300 crowd. The celebrations were loud, emotional and global. Champagne Supernova for Mayo Oasis frontmen Liam and Noel Gallagher are not exactly known for agreeing on much, but they both took to social media platform X on Sunday evening to celebrate Mayo's win. Their mother Peggy's family hails from Mayo and the Gallagher brothers spent many summers staying with their Irish relatives. "Finally!! Up Mayo!!," Noel posted, while Liam shared his congratulations, adding he was "very proud". Irish rugby legend Brian O'Driscoll and the golfer Shane Lowry also posted on social media celebrating the win. O'Driscoll said: "What a ballsy win for Mayo after that Kerry start - considering their final history. The whole country outside of The Kingdom shouting for them! Won't be a cow milked etc etc… Enjoy the celebrations." The Canadian Prime Minister, Mark Carney posted he is "proud to have roots in County Mayo". Former footballer Kevin Kilbane, who won 110 caps for the Republic of Ireland, also paid tribute to the team saying: "This was way more more than just a win to the people of Mayo!" Although he was born and grew up in England, Kilbane posted on X about the "deep love for Mayo GAA" which had been "passed down through generations". He said many had lived their whole lives without ever seeing an All-Ireland win for their county, including his own father Patrick who was born just days after the 1951 victory. Kilbane added: "To a county decimated with emigration for centuries but always having a love for home. This one is for its people." Kobe McDonald and Jordan Flynn The Gallagher brothers were not the only siblings celebrating on Sunday. On the pitch were Kobe McDonald and Jordan Flynn. At only 18 years old, McDonald made his senior football debut for Mayo in February this year. He was following in the footsteps of not only his half-brother Flynn, but also his dad Ciarán McDonald, who represented the county in three All-Ireland finals. "It's surreal, we don't know how to feel," McDonald said on the GAA Social. "To look around and see the people, they have given us so much over the years and to give them something proper to shout about is special." When asked if he knew what lay ahead in the celebrations, he added: "I don't, but I can't wait to find out. "We'll soak it in and enjoy it." In May 2026, Arsenal won the Premier League title. It had been 22 years. In June 2026, the New York Knicks won the NBA championship. It had been 53 years. For Mayo fans, the wait had been even longer. And the celebrations are only just beginning. The woman promoting the Potteries to Japan - Published A woman has been praised for her efforts in promoting the city of Stoke-on-Trent to Japan. Yuri Kawakami-Shotton runs Peak and Pottery Tours at the city's Spode Museum, showcasing the region and the Potteries to overseas visitors from Japan. She said she was inspired to spread the word about the city after watching a BBC News report about pottery firms falling into administration. "My father-in-law said: 'Oh, because no one's buying a dinner set anymore'," she explained. "And I said, 'Japanese people would buy, Japanese people would go to the museum and things. I can do that, I can maybe promote it for this city'." Kawakami-Shotton said, since starting her tours, the dinner sets made in England have proved to be a hit in Japan. "My customers love it and then some of them, for example, they come in Spode, they can't move, in front of the entrance, like 'oh my god i'm in Stoke, i'm in Spode'," she beamed. "It's like a legend." Michael Escolme, manager of the Spode Museum, praised Kawakami-Shotton's efforts to broaden their reach. "She's been a valued member of our team really, ever since bringing Japanese visitors to us both in real life and virtually to the museum," he said. Kawakami-Shotton also brings her visitors to The Rabbit Hole Tea Room in the city. In 2023, she helped the firm take their afternoon tea to Japan, where one part of the menu proved to be very popular. "We were given the amazing opportunity to go and work out at Nihonbashi in Japan where we had a pop-up of The Rabbit Hole in September," said Lee Greenhalgh, the cafe's owner. "That was insane - we went from selling a few hundred scones a day to 2,000 scones a day!" item.title: The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxqlkrlj7no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label - Published New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city. The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested courtyards on foot to hand deliver messages), its own law enforcement (burly prisoners who help stretched guards police the facility) and market (a string of stalls where convicts sell and buy goodies, like fried cassava and beignet pastries). Basically, the occupants of New Bell have adapted the jail's slack laws to work for them. The clearest example of this spirit is Jail Time Records, an on-site music studio and label making mini stars out of the most talented prisoners. Empereur, the feared leader of gangs inside and outside of the prison, has amassed 24,000 YouTube views with a music video filmed entirely in prison. Songs from the inmates have gained fans from as far away as South Africa, the US and Argentina, while earlier this year Jail Time Records put on a huge concert for the prisoners in New Bell's courtyard. "It's this instrument of resistance… where we can really share friendship, love and our voices can be heard," Steve Happi, the former inmate who co-founded Jail Time Records, tells the BBC's Talking Movies programme. "We don't think anymore about the four walls - we find the freedom." The Jail Time Records studio is rudimentary - a small, sweaty recording booth attached to a room inhabited by a solitary computer. But it is also the site of great catharsis and creativity, as per a recent, acclaimed documentary named after the studio. Directed by Happi and Italian artist Dione Roach, his Jail Time Records co-founder, it was filmed in New Bell over six years. Last month it won three prizes, including best documentary feature, at New York's Tribeca film festival. In the film, a prisoner named Stone raps into the studio's microphone: "Heart of stone, it's war. My senses shatter like broken glass. "I'm closed and tight like a cell door. No solid ground I slip like a fish." Stone, who used to be a soldier in Cameroon's presidential guard, was sentenced to 10 years in New Bell for robbery and illegal possession of firearms. He insists he is not guilty. The film captures him trying - often unsuccessfully - to reach his young daughter Maira on the phone. "It's been a long time. She needs to hear my voice from time to time, so she doesn't forget about her father," he says in a voice message to a family member, after failing to get through to Maira yet again. The music video for Heart of Stone is a typical Jail Time Records affair. The production value is high, storytelling is captivating and hordes of fellow inmates get involved as actors and crew. "The music that comes out of there is amazing," says Taika Waititi, the New Zealand Oscar-winning director who, with his wife, the singer Rita Ora, served as an executive producer for the Jail Time Records documentary. "Just in terms of the power of art in relation to redemption and what that can mean to someone who, you know, some of these people are in prison for life. I think having an outlet is an incredibly powerful and humane thing," he says. Jail Time Records was founded in 2018, when Roach volunteered for a non-profit organisation running events inside New Bell. During a dance class for the prisoners, a crew of rappers took over the microphone and began freestyling. Impressed by their performance, she asked the prison authorities for permission to start up a studio. The powers that be were receptive and so Roach enlisted Happi to run the studio as a producer and sound engineer. According to Happi, he ended up in New Bell following a family argument over what should be done with his late father's body. Amid the dispute, his aunt, a high court judge, allegedly arranged for him to be thrown into jail for killing his father. He was acquitted of the crime two years later, Jail Time Records says. In 2022, Happi, Roach and the prisoners released an album named Jail Time Vol 1. As is customary for Jail Time Records' music, half the profit from the album's sale went to the artists and the rest was reinvested into the label. The studio's survival is paramount to many of the artists, especially given New Bell's bitter environment. In 2022, Human Rights Watch reported that New Bell was housing 4,700 prisoners within its crumbling walls - four times its capacity. The prison's packed population, along with its unsanitary conditions, enabled cholera to spread rapidly during an outbreak four years ago, rights groups have said. At least six inmates died from the disease. New Bell also has a reputation for violence. In 2008, guards shot 16 inmates dead during an attempted breakout. Prisoners also attack and intimidate each other - the documentary captures Empereur, who is serving 10 years for multiple crimes, shaking down a bewildered young inmate for a necklace chain and some flip-flops. Asked if the Jail Time Records project might glorify Empereur, the son of a traditional Douala chief, and other criminals who have committed violent crimes, Roach tells the BBC: "The process we're doing is a rehabilitation process, basically. "We enter the prison without any judgment and it's the only way we can really approach this kind of work. "Music, as with any creative process, is also a way of self-discovery... coming to terms with things you've done and hopefully changing for the better". The prison authorities appear to share this view. "They were really welcoming of the project. Cameroon is a super musical country… everyone loves music," Happi says, adding that the head of the prison attended this year's concert and proceeded to dance with the performers. With official support, Jail Time Records has been able to flourish, offering opportunities to more prisoners, including those in New Bell's women's wing. Jeje, Jail Time Records first female artist, made her debut in 2022 with brooding Afrobeats song Show Me The Way. "Nobody show me the way, nobody show me the way, I did it all alone," sings Jeje, who was jailed after stealing money and running away from an allegedly abusive uncle. As well as working with the women's wing, Jail Time Records have expanded their project outside New Bell and Cameroon. Roach and Happi set up a studio 1,000 miles (1,600km) away in 2023, in the central prison of Burkina Faso's capital city, Ouagadougou. Jail Time Records hopes it can replicate the success of the original New Bell studio, with its accompanying label, music video production arm and now, award-winning documentary. The film ends with an "in memoriam" sequence; a tribute to six prisoners who died while the Jail Time Records project has been running. New Bell may appear to be endlessly bleak, but according to Happi, music provides the inmates with a "lantern for a brighter future". "Before that, they had the stubborn mentality: it's them against the world," he says. "They feel now important - they feel like they have a place in the society." What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack - Published One woman has been killed and at least 29 others injured after a van was driven into a crowd at a Berlin Pride event on Saturday night, in what officials say was likely an "Islamist terror attack". The suspect, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, has been shot and killed during a police operation in west Berlin. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has condemned the incident as a "heinous" attack. Here is what we know so far. What happened in the Berlin Pride attack? The attack happened at about 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT). A report was made to police in Berlin that a white vehicle had been driven into crowds at a Pride event in the capital. Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered at Tiergarten park, near the iconic Brandenburg Gate, for the annual event, which is known as Christopher Street Day. Some people were also stabbed in the incident, with a blade officials believe could have been a machete. Shortly afterwards, the Pride event was cancelled. A performance was abruptly brought to a end, with organisers taking to the stage and advising the crowd to start walking towards the exits. As the message was being given to the crowd, the word "evacuation" was projected onto a large screen on the stage. Unverified video posted to social media showed large crowds of people leaving the scene as emergency vehicles raced to the scene. At about 01:00 local time, police confirmed that one woman had been killed and many more had suffered injuries. A short time later, police confirmed they had found the vehicle believed to have been used in the attack, saying it had crashed into a tree. The vehicle is believed to have been rented. At about 03:30, police said on X they had identified a suspect with Islamist links. The search area was widened to the entire city and involved thousands of police, including officers from surrounding German states. On Sunday, police officers stood guard outside an apartment block in Berlin's Tiergarten district, which is said to be the suspect's home. Police say he was later shot and killed at an allotment complex in Spandau, a borough in the west of the capital, after he rushed at officers with a knife. Who is the suspect in the Berlin Pride attack? The suspect has been named by police as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese background. He was known to police and had been radicalised, officials said. A statement released by the Berlin public prosecutor's office revealed further details about Ballout's criminal history. In May 2025, prosecutors said he travelled via Turkey to Lebanon, with the intention of joining the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria. While in Lebanon he allegedly made contact with several individuals he believed were members of IS. He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict. Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention. In May this year, he was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state". The decision was deferred for six months and he was placed under the supervision of a parole officer. He was previously convicted of assault and robbery in 2022, and of robbing a victim of headphones in 2020. Where did the attack happen? The attack took place in the popular Tiergarten park, near the Brandenberg Gate. A large number of people and floats took part in the Christopher Street Day event, which passed through the city, before moving through Tiergarten park, past the Victory Column monument, and towards the Brandenberg Gate. Berlin Police have said people were hit on Ahornsteig, which is a long path stretching across the park, largely in a forested area. European leaders have been swift to condemn the attack. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed her sympathy to the victims, saying the Pride event stands for "freedom, dignity, and equality - the fundamental values of the EU". "Every person should be able to live, love, and stand up for their rights without fear," she wrote on social media. Rob Jetten, prime minister of the Netherlands, said the Dutch stand "shoulder to shoulder with our German neighbours", while Italy's prime minister Georgia Meloni expressed "solidarity and sincere sympathy". The UK's defence secretary Wes Streeting called the incident "an absolutely horrific disaster", adding his thoughts and prayers are with the German people. Did you attend Berlin Pride? Watch: Protesters celebrate resignation of India's education minister Protesters in India are celebrating after the resignation of the country's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands of young people had been demonstrating in Delhi, demanding Pradhan resign after exam paper leaks and testing irregularities. Now Pradhan has resigned, the protests organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been called off. CJP is a national movement born out of a satirical campaign, rather than an actual party, and has faced heavy police crackdowns. India cockroach protests: Videos show officers firing 'pellet guns' Thousands of people have taken to the streets in the Indian capital Delhi as part of the cockroach protests, calling for educational reforms and the resignation of a government minister.
